claims.text: The relevant material is a refractory W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf high-entropy alloy.
The as-deposited or annealed alloy has an average grain size of approximately 24–26 nm.
The initial alloy is a homogeneously disordered solid solution.
The intervention uses simultaneous 1 MeV Kr+ and 16 keV He+ irradiation at approximately 1173 K, reaching about 8.5 dpa and 9% He.
Dual-beam irradiation produces cascade events in the alloy.
Dual-beam irradiation causes grain refinement and consequently increases grain-boundary density.
Irradiation cascades fragment larger grains into sub-cascades that produce the refined microstructure.
The increased density of grain boundaries impedes dislocation motion.
Suppression of precipitation produces a more uniform solid solution.
Grain-boundary strengthening and precipitation suppression together govern and enhance hardness and strength.
Dual-beam irradiation reduces average grain size from approximately 26 nm to approximately 21 nm.
Dual-beam irradiation increases nanoindentation hardness from approximately 13–16 GPa to approximately 20 GPa.
The unirradiated or annealed baseline has larger grains and lower hardness than the irradiated sample.
The proposed mechanism applies to similarly processed refractory high-entropy alloys near 1173 K, particularly near their order-disorder transition temperature.
Marked composition changes, lower irradiation temperatures, or dominant precipitation hardening may cause deviations from the proposed behavior.
Elemental segregation, short-range ordering, and defect clustering may also contribute to hardness.
TEM grain-size measurements and nanoindentation can compare an annealed control with a nominally identical dual-beam-irradiated specimen.
Absence of significant grain refinement, absence of a hardness increase correlated with refinement, or dominance of precipitation-related changes would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The conditions call for annealed and irradiated samples to have identical temperature and dose conditions, whereas the baseline and experimental design define the control as unirradiated. An unirradiated control cannot have the same irradiation dose as the irradiated specimen.
